Hi /v/mathematics,

I'm a product owner in the software industry and I get a ton of exposure to great people who do cool things with code all the time. Me, I code a little for a couple of pet projects that speed up my workflow but it no longer holds my interest.

Recently I started to understand that mathematics and physics can be used to describe the real world. And this really grabs my interest.

But, having been completely uninterested in this drily presented topic at school I have almost zero solid foundation. As a result I'd love to know if you guys can recommend a syllabus of sorts.
For fledgling mathematicians who missed out on education, where's a good place to start?

Hi! I had no interest in math after failing trig in high school, and now I help run a math meetup group. My suggestion is to start reading. Godel, Escher, Bach is a classic, and I would suggest Ian Stewart's puzzle books. Currently our group is working through Induction and Analysis by George Poyla, which has a heavy focus on heuristics and problem solving. The Unimaginable Mathematics of Jorge Luis Borges library of Babel is an excellent place for some basics in all the areas of math. Honestly, check out the MAA website for more books.
Khan Academy is built just for this type of scenario. Check it out!

Just go to Kahn Academy, and build your knowledge base from Calculus on up, this also includes Physics... though that you might want to start from the beginning ideas of Newton's law, and if you feel the urge move onto Modern Physics.

Interesting question. Death penalty is a coward act, so I believe in that situation no one will be executed unless he/she is a real motherfucker person.
I believe executions would happen more frequently. On this topic I recommend a book called the Lucifer Effect, by Philip Zimbardo.

Yeah it would probably lead to fewer death sentence. However, just remember how infrequently the death penalty actually is doled out.

The amount of legal baggage that comes with it typically makes it a fiscally irresponsible alternative to just life without parole - which is already stupidly expensive. That's why I'm against capital punishment - the cost of the mandatory appeals process.

But your question is interesting. To pile on to it, what if the sentence was executed immediately following the judgement. Like still in the court room everyone has to press the button/lever. Or even just by casting your vote yes or no by pulling 2 different levers.

On one hand it could result in more death penalty cases. It could allow for less appeals and faster executions, which makes it a cheaper option. Also any time you get a group of people together they stop thinking like an individual and start thinking like a group. Groups of people can be violent and illogical. It might be easier for a group of 14 people to justify killing someone than for 1 individual to do it.

On the other hand if you could somehow make the person pulling the lever look at the person they are killing and tell them "I am going to kill you because..." before they had to pull the lever, it puts personal responsibility in the path of the execution and might make it harder to do.

Personally I'm against the death penalty. I see it as wasteful. Instead of killing them we should do SOMETHING with them. Use them for science, use them for labor, use them for SOMETHING.

Killing someone is insanely wasteful, for any reason.

I personally think most people who are pro-death penalty are so because of revenge fetishes and/or schadenfreude, "you've hurt this person so now I get to hurt you". It achieves nothing at all, its just revenge.
